summary: Defines the Expedited Forwarding per-hop behavior, a building block of Differentiated Services for low delay, low jitter, and low loss by serving an aggregate at a configured rate. It obsoletes RFC 2598. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Expedited Forwarding defines how one router should treat packets marked for this behavior. Its equations make service rate and packet delay measurable, but they do not define a complete path-wide service.

questions: what is the ef phb codepoint
how does ef bound delay and jitter
subtitle: A per-router forwarding behavior with measurable service-rate and packet-delay bounds.

tldr.problem: Traffic needing low delay, jitter, and loss needs a precise forwarding behavior that can be measured independently of other traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A node serves the EF traffic aggregate at a configured rate and must keep actual packet departures within defined error bounds of ideal departure times.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3246 replaces RFC 2598 with a more formal definition. It specifies a single-node behavior, not an end-to-end service.

today: RFC 3246 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2598. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 3246.

sections.title: What Expedited Forwarding Is For
sections.content:
Differentiated Services nodes use a codepoint in the IP header to select a per-hop behavior. RFC 3246 defines Expedited Forwarding (EF) as a building block intended to support services with low delay, jitter, and loss.

EF specifies one node's behavior; a separate Per-Domain Behavior may describe a group of nodes. EF is optional for a Differentiated Services node, but a node claiming EF support must conform to this specification. RFC 3246 replaces RFC 2598.
sections.plainLanguage: EF describes a marked packet's treatment at one router. A network service needs additional rules to describe how several routers work together.

sections.title: The Ideal Service Rate
sections.content:
A node should serve EF packets on an output interface at or above a configured rate, regardless of non-EF traffic. The RFC defines an ideal departure time for each packet and measures how far the actual departure falls behind it.

This approach handles both empty queues and queued packets. It avoids choosing one measurement interval for the rate and accounts for the time each packet spends waiting and being transmitted at the configured rate.
sections.plainLanguage: The router has a target finish time for each EF packet. The specification measures how late the actual finish is compared with that target.

sections.title: Aggregate and Individual Packet Bounds
sections.content:
The first equation pair describes the EF aggregate and limits departure-time error by E_a. A second pair follows each arriving packet to its own departure and limits its error by E_p.

Both pairs use the configured rate R, packet arrival and departure times, and packet length measured as the IP datagram without lower-layer overhead. The equations characterize one device; they are not alternative operating modes.
sections.plainLanguage: One error value describes how smoothly the router serves the group of EF packets. Another describes how late an individual packet may be.

sections.title: Delay, Jitter and Packet Loss
sections.content:
Smaller error values mean service stays closer to the ideal schedule. If the total EF input is bounded by a token bucket with rate r no greater than R and depth B, the RFC gives a delay bound of D = B/R + E_p. That delay bound also bounds jitter.

A device with finite buffers may still discard packets under enough load. Conformance testing checks the equations for packets that leave the device; the RFC does not specify which packets are lost.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet error bound and a limit on incoming bursts can be used to calculate a delay limit. Finite buffers can still drop packets when traffic is high enough.

sections.title: Marking and Interaction with Other Traffic
sections.content:
Codepoint 101110 is RECOMMENDED for EF. A domain should not promote or demote EF packets to another per-hop behavior, and a single microflow should not normally be reordered.

If EF uses a priority mechanism that can block other traffic without limit, the node MUST limit the harm, for example with a token bucket. The administrator must be able to configure the maximum EF rate and, where appropriate, burst size.
sections.plainLanguage: The recommended codepoint identifies EF packets. A router must also limit EF traffic when its scheduling method could otherwise prevent other traffic from being served.

sections.title: Protecting the EF Service
sections.content:
The edge of a Differentiated Services domain SHOULD police EF packets against a rate agreed with the neighboring domain and drop traffic above that rate. If no rate was agreed, the downstream domain should use a rate of zero.

Ingress traffic conditioning must ensure that only packets eligible for EF inside the domain receive the corresponding codepoint. This limits denial-of-service and theft-of-service risks.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain should check EF traffic at its boundary and enforce the agreed rate. This prevents unapproved traffic from taking the EF treatment.

sections.title: Implementation Examples
sections.content:
The non-normative appendix compares scheduling approaches. It describes a priority queue in a suitable output-buffered device as a way to achieve low aggregate and packet error, while noting that a non-EF packet already being transmitted cannot be preempted.

Weighted round robin may provide a lower supported EF rate and a larger aggregate error. Hierarchical scheduling can reorder packets within EF and may make a useful individual-packet error bound difficult to state.
sections.plainLanguage: Different schedulers can meet the EF equations with different error bounds. The appendix gives examples, but does not require one particular scheduler.
